question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should both operators do?
choice_a: The larger vessel always has right-of-way regardless of position
choice_b: Each should alter course to starboard (right) so they pass port-to-port
choice_c: Both should stop and wait for instructions
choice_d: Each should alter course to port (left) so they pass starboard-to-starboard
explanation: In a head-on meeting, the Navigation Rules direct each power-driven vessel to alter course to starboard, passing each other port side to port side.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), meeting situations

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the give-way vessel?
choice_c: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own starboard (right) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel on its own port (left) side
explanation: When two power-driven vessels cross, the vessel that sees the other on its starboard side must give way and take early, substantial action to avoid collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), crossing situations

question: In a crossing situation, what must the stand-on vessel generally do?
choice_c: Speed up to cross ahead of the give-way vessel
choice_d: Maintain its course and speed unless a collision becomes imminent
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed so the give-way vessel can maneuver predictably, only taking evasive action if collision becomes unavoidable otherwise.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), crossing situations

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel must always give way, regardless of whether it is under sail or power?
choice_a: The vessel that is overtaking (coming up from behind) another vessel
choice_d: The sailing vessel, even if it is being overtaken by a powerboat
explanation: Regardless of vessel type, the overtaking vessel is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel it is passing until well clear.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), overtaking situations

question: As a general rule, which type of vessel has right-of-way over a power-driven vessel that is not restricted in its ability to maneuver?
choice_a: Any vessel that departed the dock first
choice_b: A sailing vessel operating under sail alone
explanation: A sailing vessel under sail generally has right-of-way over an ordinary power-driven vessel, although exceptions exist, such as when the sailing vessel is overtaking or the power vessel is restricted in its ability to maneuver.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), sail vs. power priority

question: One short blast of a horn from an operating vessel signals what intention under the Navigation Rules?
choice_b: Danger, or I do not understand your intentions
choice_c: I intend to leave you on my port side / I am altering course to starboard
explanation: One short blast signals a course change to starboard (or intent to pass port-to-port); two short blasts signal a turn to port, and three short blasts indicate operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), sound signals

question: What does a signal of five or more short, rapid horn blasts mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_d: A danger signal, or an indication that the operator does not understand or agree with the other vessel's intentions
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger/doubt signal, warning the other vessel of a hazard or that its intentions are unclear.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), sound signals

question: A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, such as one engaged in dredging or laying cable, generally has right-of-way over what kind of vessel?
choice_a: A vessel that is otherwise under power and not restricted in its ability to maneuver
choice_d: No other vessel; restricted vessels always give way
explanation: Vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver rank above ordinary power-driven vessels in the right-of-way hierarchy because they cannot readily take evasive action.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), vessel priority hierarchy

question: What action should the give-way vessel take when required to keep clear of another vessel?
choice_a: Do nothing and let the stand-on vessel maneuver instead
choice_b: Take early and substantial action, altering course and/or speed enough to be obviously noticeable to the other vessel
choice_c: Wait until the last possible moment, then make a small, subtle adjustment
choice_d: Speed up to pass ahead as quickly as possible
explanation: The Navigation Rules require the give-way vessel to act early and make its avoidance maneuver large enough to be clearly recognized by the other vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), general responsibilities

question: Under the Navigation Rules, which vessel is generally given right-of-way over a personal watercraft or motorboat: a vessel actively engaged in commercial fishing with gear deployed, or an ordinary recreational boat?
choice_a: Whichever vessel is closer to a marked channel
choice_b: Neither; fishing vessels have no special status
choice_c: The vessel actively engaged in commercial fishing with gear out and restricted in its ability to maneuver
choice_d: The recreational boat, since it is smaller and more maneuverable
explanation: A vessel engaged in fishing with gear deployed that restricts its maneuverability generally ranks above an ordinary recreational power-driven vessel in the right-of-way hierarchy.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), vessel priority hierarchy

question: What is the Navigation Rules' definition of 'overtaking'?
choice_a: Approaching another vessel from directly ahead
choice_b: Passing another vessel while both are stationary
choice_c: Any time one vessel is faster than another, regardless of position
choice_d: Approaching another vessel from more than 22.5 degrees abaft (behind) her beam
explanation: A vessel is considered to be overtaking when it approaches another from more than 22.5 degrees abaft that vessel's beam, essentially from behind and to the side.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), overtaking definition

question: What is the general 'rule of common sense' boaters are taught alongside the formal right-of-way rules?
choice_a: Every operator must do whatever is necessary to avoid a collision, even if it means departing from the standard rules
choice_b: The stand-on vessel must never alter course under any circumstances
choice_c: Right-of-way rules only apply during daylight hours
choice_d: Right-of-way rules only apply to vessels over 26 feet
explanation: The Navigation Rules include a general prudence provision: no rule excuses an operator from taking whatever action is needed to avoid an actual collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), Rule 2, general prudential rule

question: On narrow channels, which vessel is generally required to keep to the outer edge of the channel that lies on her starboard side, and stay as far to that side as safe?
choice_b: Every vessel proceeding along the channel
explanation: In a narrow channel or fairway, every vessel must keep as near the outer limit of the channel on her starboard side as is safe and practicable.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), narrow channel rule

question: A vessel should never impede the passage of what kind of vessel in a narrow channel, if that vessel can only navigate safely within the channel?
choice_b: There is no such rule for narrow channels
choice_c: A large vessel that can only operate safely within the narrow channel
explanation: A smaller, more maneuverable vessel should avoid impeding a larger vessel that can only navigate safely within the confines of a narrow channel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), narrow channel rule

question: What does 'restricted visibility' (fog, heavy rain, haze) require of vessel operators under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: Increasing speed to clear the area faster
choice_b: Turning off all lights to avoid confusing other vessels
choice_c: No special action is required if operating a small recreational boat
choice_d: Proceeding at a safe speed adapted to the conditions and sounding appropriate fog signals
explanation: In restricted visibility, all vessels must reduce to a safe speed for conditions and use the prescribed sound signals to alert others of their presence.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), conduct in restricted visibility

question: What does two short horn blasts from a power-driven vessel signal to another vessel during a meeting or crossing situation?
choice_a: I intend to leave you on my starboard side / I am altering course to port
choice_b: I am altering course to starboard
choice_c: I am backing down (operating astern propulsion)
choice_d: I am anchored and unable to move
explanation: Two short blasts communicate an intended turn to port, signaling the operator will leave the other vessel on their starboard side.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR 83), sound signals
